title: How Data Centers Can Prepare for Hurricane Season Without Losing Power
excerpt: Data center power demand is already outpacing the grid. Add hurricane season and the risk compounds. Here's what real preparedness looks like for a data center campus.

content.text: Data centers were already running into a power problem before hurricane season became part of the conversation. U.S. data center power demand is projected to climb from 31 gigawatts in 2025 to 41 gigawatts in 2026, and to roughly 66 gigawatts by 2027, according to Goldman Sachs Research. That growth is arriving faster than new grid capacity can be built to meet it.

Layer a hurricane season on top of a grid that is already stretched thin, and the risk compounds. Here is what that risk actually looks like for a data center campus, and what preparedness requires when standard grid capacity is no longer a safe assumption.
The Grid Problem Existed Before the Storm Problem

Interconnection delays are becoming the norm for large-load customers, not the exception. S&P Global's research on the U.S. data center power crunch found that customer-sited, on-site power resources now offer a faster path to capacity than waiting for new grid-connected supply â€” a shift driven by the pace of AI-related demand outrunning what utilities can deliver on a workable timeline. That means many data center campuses are already evaluating on-site generation for capacity reasons alone, before weather ever enters the conversation.
What an Outage Actually Costs a Data Center

The financial stakes of losing power at a data center are not abstract. Industry estimates place the cost of data center downtime at roughly $9,000 per minute, and a full day of downtime at a major facility has been estimated to exceed $12 million, according to figures compiled by Bloom Energy and Empower IT Services. For hyperscale facilities supporting AI workloads, per-hour costs during an extended outage can run into the millions once cascading effects on dependent customers and service-level agreements are factored in.

Those numbers do not require a direct hit from a hurricane to materialize. A regional grid failure, a damaged substation, or an extended utility restoration timeline after a storm passes nearby can produce the same outcome.
Hurricane Season Adds a Second Layer of Risk

NOAA's official outlook for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, which runs June 1 through November 30, calls for a below-average year: 8 to 14 named storms, with 3 to 6 expected to become hurricanes and 1 to 3 reaching major hurricane strength. A below-average forecast is not the same as a low-risk season, and NOAA has been direct about that distinction. As National Weather Service Director Ken Graham put it when the outlook was released, "It only takes one."

content.text: For a data center campus, one storm affecting the regional grid is enough to turn a capacity-planning problem into an operational one, especially for facilities already running close to their interconnection limits.

Preparedness for a data center campus is not a generator sized for a brief outage. It is a power architecture built to operate independent of the grid it would otherwise be waiting on before, during, and after a storm. That requires:

items: On-site, behind-the-meter power that does not depend on utility restoration timelines.
A platform that scales with campus load rather than functioning as a stopgap measure.
A fuel input that isn't competing with the rest of the region for the same delivery trucks after a storm.
